extraction_notes.note: The tagged displays (P), (G), (G'), (DG'), (G''), (DG''), (Q), (Q'), (DQ'), (BIL), (LIN) are numbered equation environments whose content is an optimization formulation; typed problem (Hard rule 4 promotion) rather than equation, confidence 0.9.

(P) is displayed twice with the same tag: the introduction states it over a generic class F, Section 2.2 over convex C^{1,1}_L functions. Treated as two problems (ProbP3 specializes ProbP1) instead of one repeated statement, since the function classes differ.
Numbered equations (2.1-style GM rate and Nesterov's FGM rate) retyped as external theorems: the text presents each as the known convergence rate of a cited method.

The appendix proof of Lemma 3.3 is split by subsections A.1 (S_0) and A.2 (S_1); emitted as two proof nodes, both proving LP3, with a uses edge from the second part to the first. The one-sentence section-A preamble is not in either node.

The feasibility remark for (BIL) cites the proof of Theorem 3.2 (T:gradLowBound), but the explicit dual feasible point is given in the proof of Theorem 3.1; the \ref edge from TP3 stays and a uses edge from PP3 was added.
Numerical bounds for HBM, FGM and the optimized method are given only as tables and a plot inside figures; the tables are not nodes, and the prose conclusions drawn from them are numerical claims.

The intermediate unnumbered relaxed PEP formulations in Section 3.1, the epsilon-optimality sentence (never used again), and the N=5 optimal-step algorithm shown in a figure were not extracted as nodes.
Algorithms are written as enumerate lists in \fbox rather than algorithm environments, so they are prose algorithm nodes; GM and FO have a single iteration line and get no steps.

nodes.statement: subsectionA General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples As before, our family F is the class of convex functions in C^1,1_L(R^d), and \d,N,L, R\ are fixed. Consider the following class of first-order methods: fboxparbox14cm Algorithm FO setcounterenumi-1 item Input: fin C^1,1_L(R^d), x_0in R^d. item For i=0,dots,N-1, compute x_i+1 = x_i - frac1L sum_k=0^i h^(i+1)_k f^prime(x_k). Here, h_k^(i) in R play the role of step-sizes, which we assume to be fixed and determined by the algorithm. The interest in the analysis of first-order algorithms of this type is motivated by the fact that it covers some fundamental first-order schemes beyond the gradient method. In particular, to motivate (FO), let us consider the following two algorithms which are of particular interest, and as we shall see below can be seen as special cases of (FO). We start with the so-called Heavy Ball Method (HBM). For earlier work on this method see Polyak , and for some interesting modern developments and applications, we refer the reader to Attouch et al. and references therein. The Heavy Ball Method (HBM) fboxparbox14cm Algorithm HBM setcounterenumi-1 item Input: fin C^1,1_L(R^d), x_0in R^d, item x_1 leftarrow x_0 - fracalphaL f^prime(x_0) item For i=1,dots,N-1 compute: x_i+1 = x_i - fracalphaL f^prime(x_i) +beta (x_i-x_i-1) Here the step sizes alpha and beta are chosen such that 0 leq beta < 1 and 0 < alpha < 2(1+beta), see . By recursively eliminating the term x_i-x_i-1 in step 2 of HBM, we can rewrite this step as \[ x_i+1= x_i - frac1L sum_k=0^i alpha beta^i-k f^prime(x_k), i=1,dots,N-1. \] Therefore, the heavy ball method is a special case of Algorithm~FOxspace with the choice h^(i+1)_k= alpha beta^i-k, k=0, ldots, i, \; i=0, ldots N-1 . The next algorithm is Nesterov's celebrated Fast Gradient Method . The fast gradient method (FGM) fboxparbox14cm Algorithm FGM setcounterenumi-1 item Input: fin C^1,1_L(R^d), x_0in R^d, item y_1 leftarrow x_0, t_1 leftarrow 1, item For i=1,dots,N compute: item x_i leftarrow y_i -frac1L f^prime(y_i), item t_i+1 leftarrow frac1+sqrt1+4 t_i^22, item y_i+1 leftarrow x_i + fract_i-1t_i+1(x_i-x_i-1). A major breakthrough was achieved by Nesterov in , where he proved that the FGM, which requires almost no increase in computational effort when compared to the basic gradient scheme, achieves the improved rate of convergence O(1/N^2) for function values. More precisely, one hasfootnoteThe bound given here, which improves the original bound derived in , was recently obtained in Beck-Teboulle . f(x_N)-f^ast leq frac2L\|x_0-x_ast\|^2(N+1)^2, forall x_ast in X_ast(f). The order of complexity of Nesterov's algorithm is also optimal, as it is possible to show that there exists a convex function fin C^1,1_L(R^d) such that when dgeq 2N+1, and under some other mild assumptions, any first-order algorithm that generates a point x_N by performing N calls to a first-order oracle of f satisfies \[ f(x_N)-f^ast geq frac3L \|x_0-x_ast\|^232(N+1)^2, forall x_ast in X_ast(f). \] This fundamental algorithm discovered about 30 years ago by Nesterov has been recently revived and is currently subject of intensive research activities. For some of its extensions and many applications, see e.g., the recent survey paper Beck-Teboulle and references therein. At first glance, Algorithm~FGM seems different than the scheme FOxspace defined above. Here two sequences are defined: the main sequence x_0,dots,x_N and an auxiliary sequence y_1,dots,y_N. Observing that the gradient of the function is only evaluated on the auxiliary sequence of points \y_i\, we show in the next proposition that FGM fits in the scheme FOxspace through the following algorithm: fboxparbox14cm Algorithm FGM^primexspace setcounterenumi-1 item Input: fin C^1,1_L(R^d), x_0in R^d, item y_1 leftarrow x_0, item For i=1,dots,N-1 compute: itemy_i+1 leftarrow y_i -frac1L sum_k=1^i h^(i+1)_k f^prime(y_k), item x_N leftarrow y_N -frac1L f^prime(y_N), with h^(i+1)_k = fract_i-1t_i+1h^(i)_k & k+2leq i, \\ fract_i-1t_i+1(h^(i)_i-1-1) & k = i-1, \\ 1+fract_i-1t_i+1 & k = i (i=1,dots,N-1, \ k=1,dots,i). and t_i = 1 & i=1 \\ frac1+sqrt1+4 t_i-1^22 & i>1. The points y_1,dots,y_N,x_N generated by Algorithm~FGM^primexspace are identical to the respective points generated by Algorithm~FGMxspace. We will show by induction that the sequence y_i generated by Algorithm~FGM^primexspace is identical to the sequence y_i generated by Algorithm~FGMxspace, and that the value of x_N generated by Algorithm~FGM^primexspace is equal to the value of x_N generated by Algorithm~FGMxspace. First note that the sequence t_i is defined by the two algorithms in the same way. Now let \x_i, y_i\ be the sequences generated by FGMxspace and denote by \y_i^prime\, x_N^prime the sequence generated by FGM^primexspace. Obviously, y^prime_1 = y_1 and since t_1=1 we get using the relations : y_2^prime &= y_1^prime - frac1L h^(2)_1 f^prime(y_1^prime) = y_1 - frac1L left(1+fract_1-1t_2 right) f^prime(y_1) = y_1 - frac1L f^prime(y_1)= x_1 = y_2. Consider the following class of first-order methods: fboxparbox14cm Algorithm FO setcounterenumi-1 item Input: fin C^1,1_L(R^d), x_0in R^d. item For i=0,dots,N-1, compute x_i+1 = x_i - frac1L sum_k=0^i h^(i+1)_k f^prime(x_k). Here, h_k^(i) in R play the role of step-sizes, which we assume to be fixed and determined by the algorithm. The interest in the analysis of first-order algorithms of this type is motivated by the fact that it covers some fundamental first-order schemes beyond the gradient method. In particular, to motivate (FO), let us consider the following two algorithms which are of particular interest, and as we shall see below can be seen as special cases of (FO). We start with the so-called Heavy Ball Method (HBM). For earlier work on this method see Polyak , and for some interesting modern developments and applications, we refer the reader to Attouch et al. and references therein. The Heavy Ball Method (HBM) fboxparbox14cm Algorithm HBM setcounterenumi-1 item Input: fin C^1,1_L(R^d), x_0in R^d, item x_1 leftarrow x_0 - fracalphaL f^prime(x_0) item For i=1,dots,N-1 compute: x_i+1 = x_i - fracalphaL f^prime(x_i) +beta (x_i-x_i-1) Here the step sizes alpha and beta are chosen such that 0 leq beta < 1 and 0 < alpha < 2(1+beta), see . By recursively eliminating the term x_i-x_i-1 in step 2 of HBM, we can rewrite this step as \[ x_i+1= x_i - frac1L sum_k=0^i alpha beta^i-k f^prime(x_k), i=1,dots,N-1. \] Therefore, the heavy ball method is a special case of Algorithm~FOxspace with the choice h^(i+1)_k= alpha beta^i-k, k=0, ldots, i, \; i=0, ldots N-1 . The next algorithm is Nesterov's celebrated Fast Gradient Method . The fast gradient method (FGM) fboxparbox14cm Algorithm FGM setcounterenumi-1 item Input: fin C^1,1_L(R^d), x_0in R^d, item y_1 leftarrow x_0, t_1 leftarrow 1, item For i=1,dots,N compute: item x_i leftarrow y_i -frac1L f^prime(y_i), item t_i+1 leftarrow frac1+sqrt1+4 t_i^22, item y_i+1 leftarrow x_i + fract_i-1t_i+1(x_i-x_i-1). A major breakthrough was achieved by Nesterov in , where he proved that the FGM, which requires almost no increase in computational effort when compared to the basic gradient scheme, achieves the improved rate of convergence O(1/N^2) for function values. More precisely, one hasfootnoteThe bound given here, which improves the original bound derived in , was recently obtained in Beck-Teboulle . f(x_N)-f^ast leq frac2L\|x_0-x_ast\|^2(N+1)^2, forall x_ast in X_ast(f).
